d: Explore the physical units used in Roblox and how they convert to metric units.
h:
This article outlines Roblox physical units and how they convert to metric units. Understanding units is useful whenever you work with physics, as in the following examples:

  • Tuning linear/angular velocities, forces, torques, stiffness, and damping of mechanical constraints and mover constraints.
  • Adjusting the density of custom materials.

Unit conversions

In general, you can use the conversions in the following table to relate Roblox's primary units for time, length, and mass to their metric counterparts.

Unit Roblox Metric
Time $\text{1 second}$ $\text{1 second}$
Length $\text{1 stud}$ $\text{28 cm}$
Mass $\text{1 RMU}$* $\text{21.952 kg}$

The primary units are used to generate conversions for derived units such as water density and air pressure at standard conditions. The following physical properties are expressed in metric units and Roblox units, with primary unit equivalents provided in brackets. All conversions have been rounded to three significant figures.

Unit Metric Roblox
Water density $\text{1 g/cm³}$ $\text{1 RMU/stud³}$
Air density (sea level) $\text{0.00129 g/cm³}$ $\text{0.00129 RMU/stud³}$
1 atmosphere $\text{101,325 Pa [kg/(m s²)]}$ $\text{1290 RMU/(stud s²)}$
Spring stiffness $\text{1 N/m [kg/s²]}$ $\text{0.0456 RMU/s²}$
Spring damping $\text{1 N s/m [kg/s]}$ $\text{0.0456 RMU/s}$
Velocity $\text{1 m/s}$ $\text{3.57 studs/s}$
Force $\text{1 N [kg m/s²]}$ $\text{0.163 Rowtons [RMU stud/s²]}$
Torque $\text{1 N-m [kg m²/s²]}$ $\text{0.581 Rowton-studs [RMU stud²/s²]}$

The following table illustrates gravitational acceleration in Roblox units and metric units.

Behavior Roblox Metric
Roblox default $\text{196.2 studs/s²}$ $\text{54.936 m/s²}$
Realistic (real-world) $\text{35 studs/s²}$ $\text{9.8 m/s²}$

Roblox places limits on certain physical properties, as outlined in the following table. Details on these properties is located in the PhysicalProperties documentation.

Property Minimum Maximum
Density ($\text{RMU/stud³}$) $\text{0.0001}$ $\text{100}$
Friction $\text{0.0}$ $\text{2.0}$
Friction weight $\text{0.0}$ $\text{100}$
Elasticity $\text{0.0}$ $\text{1.0}$
Elasticity weight $\text{0.0}$ $\text{100}$

Unit consistency

Internally, the Roblox physics engine does not use unit conversions. You're free to define your own unit interpretations for studs (length) and RMUs (mass), but these should be used in a consistent manner throughout the game. For example, if you decide that one stud equals one foot (30.483 cm), the unit density of water implies an RMU is equal to 62.4 lbs (28.3 kg):

$\text{1 (g/cm³)} × \text{(30.48³ cm³/ft³)} =$
$\text{28,317 (g/ft³)} × \text{(0.00220462 lbs/g)} =$
$\text{62.4 (lbs/ft³)} =$
$\text{1 (RMU/stud³)}$

Overall, it's recommended that you use standard Roblox units because it makes a game work as expected in all scenarios, such as compatibility with VR controls.

kid.simple: This page explains the measuring units Roblox physics uses, like studs for length and RMUs for mass, and how they compare to real-world units. That matters when you tune speeds, forces, springs, and materials and want them to feel right. For example, one stud is about 28 centimeters. It also shows Roblox's default gravity, which is much stronger than real Earth gravity.
kid.analogy: It is like converting between Celsius and Fahrenheit: the heat is the same, you just use a different number to describe it. Studs and meters describe the same distance with different numbers.
keyPoints: Time is the same: 1 second in Roblox is 1 real second.
Length: 1 stud equals 28 cm. So a 10-stud wall is about 2.8 meters tall.
Mass: 1 RMU (Roblox Mass Unit) equals 21.952 kg.
Speed: 1 meter per second equals 3.57 studs per second.
Force is measured in Rowtons (1 newton is 0.163 Rowtons), and torque in Rowton-studs (1 newton-meter is 0.581 Rowton-studs).
Default Roblox gravity is 196.2 studs/s², about 5.6 times stronger than real gravity. Realistic gravity is 35 studs/s².
Material settings have limits: density 0.0001 to 100, friction 0 to 2, elasticity 0 to 1, and friction or elasticity weight 0 to 100.
The engine itself does not care what a stud 'really' is, but it is best to stick with the standard Roblox units so things like VR controls work as expected.

terms.stud: Roblox's unit of length. 1 stud is 28 cm, so a 4-stud-wide part is about 1.1 meters wide.
terms.RMU: Roblox Mass Unit, the unit for how heavy something is. 1 RMU is 21.952 kg.
terms.density: How heavy something is for its size. Water is 1 RMU per cubic stud, so a 1x1x1-stud block of water-density material weighs 1 RMU.
terms.Rowton: Roblox's unit of force. 1 newton (the real-world force unit) equals 0.163 Rowtons.
terms.torque: A twisting force, measured in Rowton-studs.
terms.studs/s²: How fast speed changes each second. Gravity of 196.2 studs/s² means a falling object gains 196.2 studs per second of speed every second.
terms.spring stiffness and damping: Stiffness is how hard a spring pulls back; damping is how much it slows down bouncing.
terms.friction: How much surfaces grip. 0 is like ice; 2 is very grippy.
terms.elasticity: How bouncy something is. 0 does not bounce; 1 bounces back with almost all its energy.
terms.metric units: Real-world units like meters, kilograms, and newtons.

example.title: Switch to realistic gravity
example.code:
-- Roblox default gravity is 196.2 studs/s^2
print("Old gravity:", workspace.Gravity)

-- 35 studs/s^2 matches real Earth gravity (9.8 m/s^2)
workspace.Gravity = 35

-- Convert a real-world speed to studs per second
local metersPerSecond = 5
local studsPerSecond = metersPerSecond * 3.57
print("5 m/s is about", studsPerSecond, "studs per second")
explain: `workspace.Gravity` holds the gravity strength in studs per second squared.
Setting it to 35 makes things fall like they do in real life, which feels floatier than normal Roblox.
To turn a real speed into studs per second, multiply by 3.57, because 1 m/s equals 3.57 studs/s.

watchOut: Changing `workspace.Gravity` to realistic values makes jumps feel very floaty and high. Players' jump settings may need adjusting too.
Numbers from real-world physics will not work as-is. Convert them with the table first, or your forces will be way too strong or weak.
If you invent your own meaning for a stud (like 1 foot), use it the same way everywhere, or your physics will not match up.
